passages: Owen Pryce woke before dawn, the way he always did, to the sound of his wife Mari filling the kettle downstairs. It was the autumn of 1926, and the coal towns of the Rhondda Valley smelled of soot and rain no matter the season. He dressed by candlelight, pulled on the boots that never quite dried, and kissed his daughter Nan on the top of her head as she slept. In the kitchen, Mari pressed a tin of bread and cheese into his hands and said nothing about the strike that had ended three months before, nothing about the wages that had not recovered, because there was nothing new to say. Owen was thirty-four, broad through the shoulders, with coal dust worked so deep into the creases of his knuckles that no scrubbing brush had ever found the bottom of it. He walked the mile to the pithead with two dozen other men, their lamps swinging like slow fireflies in the dark.

Underground, the world narrowed to the width of the tunnel and the small yellow circle of lamplight. Owen worked the coal face with his butty, Rhys Bevan, a wiry man ten years his senior who sang under his breath to keep time with his own pick. The seam was tight that week, barely four feet high, and both men worked half-crouched, backs aching by the second hour. Rhys grumbled about the new props the company had sent down, thinner than the old oak ones, cut to save money rather than to hold a roof. Owen ran his hand along one and felt it flex slightly under his palm, which it should not have done. He mentioned it to the overman, who wrote something in a ledger and moved on without looking up. There was coal to bring up, a quota chalked on a board at the surface, and no shift ever ended early for a worry about timber.

By the third day, a fine trickle of dust had begun sifting down from a crack near the roof, so faint that a man had to hold his lamp close and still to see it. Rhys noticed it first and stopped singing. He told Owen they ought to shore it properly before going further, and Owen agreed, though both men understood what asking for extra timber would mean: a stopped shift, a docked wage, an argument with an overman who answered to men who had never once been underground. They compromised, as tired men do, deciding to finish the day's quota and raise it formally in the morning. Owen thought of Nan's boots, worn through at the toe, and the shillings a full quota would bring. He picked up his tool again. Somewhere above them, water that had been finding its way through old workings for weeks had already begun to change the pressure on the rock they stood beneath.

The roof came down without warning, a great cough of rock and dust that filled the tunnel from floor to ceiling in less than the time it took to draw breath. Rhys, ten feet further back, was thrown against the wall and lived. Owen did not answer when the men began shouting his name into the settling dark. It took six hours to clear enough stone to reach him, working by hand in the end because the props nearest the fall had gone too, and when they did, they found him where the largest slab had come down, and there was no question of a doctor, only of carrying him up into daylight so that his wife would not have to be told underground. Rhys carried one corner of the stretcher himself, though his own arm was broken, and would not let anyone relieve him of it until they reached the top.

Mari Pryce was hanging washing when the mine's hooter sounded twice at midday, a signal every wife in the valley had learned to dread, and she was still standing with a wet sheet in her hands when the minister's cart came up the lane. She did not scream. She set the sheet down carefully on the line, as though it mattered, and went inside to wake Nan from her nap, because she did not want her daughter to hear it from a stranger. The house filled quickly after that, the way houses did in the valley, with neighbor women bringing tea and bread and taking over the kitchen without being asked, and men standing awkwardly in the yard with their caps in their hands. Nan, five years old, asked twice when her father was coming home before she understood, from the silence that followed, that she should stop asking.

The funeral was held on a Thursday, under a sky the color of wet slate, and half the village walked behind the cart because half the village had lost someone to the pits at one time or another and knew what was owed. Rhys Bevan stood at the graveside with his arm still in a sling, and when the minister finished speaking he stepped forward and said a few words of his own, plain ones, about a good butty and a fair man, before his voice gave out. Mari stood very straight through all of it, Nan's hand gripped tightly in hers, and did not cry until the first shovel of earth went in, at which point she cried the way people cry who have been holding something back for three days. The company sent a small sum of compensation, calculated, someone said bitterly, more cheaply than new timber would have cost.

Winter came hard that year, and Mari took in washing and mending to make up what the compensation would not stretch to cover. Nan grew used to the smell of other people's linen drying by the fire and to her mother's silences, which were not unhappy exactly, only tired in a way that seemed to have settled into her bones. Rhys Bevan came by most weeks, ostensibly to check the roof and the coal store, and stayed longer each time than the checking required. He never went back underground himself after his arm healed, taking work instead at the surface, sorting coal, for wages that were smaller but came with the certainty of walking home every evening. Mari found herself, some evenings, listening for his knock before she admitted to herself that she was listening for anything at all.

By the following autumn, Rhys had taken to walking Nan to school on the mornings he wasn't needed at the yard, and the neighbors had stopped remarking on it, which in a village that size was its own kind of blessing. He asked Mari to marry him in October, plainly, over tea, the way he did everything, and she said yes before she had time to feel guilty about how quickly the word came. Nan, who called him Uncle Rhys still out of habit, would grow up calling him something else within the year. On the anniversary of the collapse, Mari walked up to the small stone in the chapel yard alone, laid a handful of late flowers against it, and stood for a while in the cold air, feeling, for the first time in a long time, something that was almost peace.

Amalia Rocha kept her kitchen exactly as her mother had kept it, with the same blue tiles and the same brass pot for boiling milk, in a fourth-floor apartment in Lisbon's Alfama district where she had lived for fifty-one years. She was seventy-eight, still climbing the steep stairs herself, though more slowly than she used to, and still making her granddaughter Sofia's favorite custard tarts every Sunday whether Sofia came or not. That particular Sunday in March, Sofia noticed her grandmother pausing halfway through kneading dough, one hand pressed flat against her side, and asked if she was all right. Amalia waved the question away the way she waved away most fuss, saying it was nothing, an old woman's stomach complaining about an old woman's life, and changed the subject to whether Sofia's boyfriend had finally proposed. But she sat down twice more before the tarts went into the oven, which she had never done before.

The doctor at the hospital in Santa Maria used the word pancreatic in a tone that told Sofia, before she understood the medical details, exactly how serious it was. Amalia listened to the diagnosis with her hands folded in her lap, asked two practical questions about timelines and treatment, and then asked whether she would still be able to go up and down her own stairs. The doctor said that depended, which they both understood to mean no, eventually. Sofia's mother, Amalia's only daughter, cried in the hospital corridor while Amalia stayed dry-eyed inside, more concerned, it seemed, with how her family would take the news than with the news itself. On the drive home she asked Sofia to stop at the market so she could buy the ingredients for a proper dinner, insisting that no one in this family was going to stop eating just because of a scan.

Amalia chose to have her treatments and, when the doctors were honest with her about what those treatments could and could not do, chose after two months to stop them. She wanted to die in the apartment on the fourth floor, she said, not in a hospital bed with strangers' machines humming around her, and her daughter, after arguing for a week, arranged for a nurse to visit and moved a proper bed into the front room where the light was good. Neighbors Amalia had known for decades took turns bringing meals none of them had the heart to eat much of. Sofia came every day after work, sometimes just to sit while her grandmother slept, sometimes to be handed instructions, delivered with surprising sharpness, about how the custard tarts were meant to be made and how badly everyone else in the family made them.

On what turned out to be one of her last clear afternoons, Amalia asked Sofia to bring the small wooden box from the top of the wardrobe, the one with her mother's recipes written on cards gone soft and brown at the corners. She went through them slowly, naming which ones Sofia's mother liked and which ones nobody had made in years, and made Sofia promise to keep the box rather than let it be thrown out during whatever clearing-up would eventually happen to the apartment. She did not say the word death, not directly, but the instructions had the shape of someone putting her affairs in order one small object at a time. Toward evening she grew tired and asked Sofia to open the window, saying she wanted to hear the street a while before she slept, and Sofia sat with her until the light outside went properly dark.

Amalia Rocha died three days later, in the early hours of the morning, with her daughter asleep in the chair beside the bed and the nurse only just gone down the hall. There had been no dramatic final moment; her breathing had simply grown further apart until it stopped altogether, and it was several minutes before anyone in the apartment realized the room had gone quiet in a different way than it had been quiet all week. Sofia arrived at seven to find her mother sitting very still, holding her grandmother's hand, and understood immediately from the stillness of the apartment itself, from the light already too bright and ordinary through the window, what had happened. The recipe box sat exactly where Amalia had left it on the bedside table, closed, as though she had tidied it away herself before going.

The funeral filled the small chapel near Alfama with people from four different decades of Amalia's life, women who had bought bread from her at the same corner store for thirty years, a cousin who had flown in from Porto, neighbors who brought, without any coordination, three separate trays of the same custard tarts made from memory and none of them quite right. Sofia's mother spoke for a long time about her own mother's stubbornness, which drew as much laughter as it did tears, and Sofia found she could not speak at all when her turn came, only stood at the front holding the recipe box against her chest until someone gently took her arm and led her back to her seat. Afterward, at the apartment, people ate and drank and told stories, and for an hour or two the rooms felt almost as full as they used to.

It took Sofia's mother four months to work up to clearing out the apartment, and when she finally did, Sofia asked to be the one to go through the kitchen. She found flour still in its tin, a shopping list in her grandmother's handwriting for a Sunday that had never come, and, tucked behind the brass pot, a photograph of Amalia as a young woman that no one in the family had ever seen. She kept the pot, the recipe box, and the photograph, and let her mother and the estate agent handle the rest of the emptying, the furniture sold or given away, the blue-tiled kitchen photographed for a listing that described it as full of character. Sofia cried harder over the empty rooms than she had at the funeral, standing in the doorway of a kitchen that no longer smelled like anything at all.

A year later, Sofia made custard tarts in her own kitchen for the first time, using her great-grandmother's recipe card and her grandmother's brass pot, for a small gathering to celebrate her daughter's first birthday. They came out slightly wrong, a little too brown at the edges, and she found herself laughing about it the way Amalia used to laugh at other people's failed attempts, understanding the joke properly for the first time. Her mother tasted one and said, with real surprise, that it was closer than anyone else had managed. Sofia set one tart aside on a small plate before the guests arrived, an old habit she couldn't explain to anyone who asked, and put it on the windowsill where the afternoon light came in, the way her grandmother used to leave one cooling there every Sunday of Sofia's whole childhood.

Silas Coombe signed articles aboard the whaling ship Amara in the spring of 1851, seventeen years old and lean as a fence rail, having told the recruiting agent he was nineteen and being believed because no one who checked such things closely. New Bedford's harbor smelled of tar and rendered oil, and Silas stood at the rail as the ropes were cast off, watching the town where his mother and his intended, a quiet young woman named Ruth Anders, both stood among the crowd on the dock. He had signed on for a share of the voyage's profits, three years at sea if the hunting was slow, and a chance to come home with enough money to marry properly instead of waiting on his father's approval, which had not been forthcoming. He did not look away from the shore until it had shrunk to a line and then to nothing at all.

Life aboard settled into a rhythm within a fortnight, one Silas found he could bear better than he had expected: the watches, the endless mending of line and canvas, the salted meat that improved not at all with familiarity. The captain, a weathered man named Obed Thatcher, ran a fair ship by the standards of the trade, quick with a rope's end for laziness but quicker still to notice a man who worked hard and reward him with easier duty when he could. Silas was assigned to one of the whaleboats under a seasoned harpooner who taught him, over weeks, how to read the sea for the telltale spout and slap of a sounding whale. His first lowering came off the coast of the Azores, a chase that ended without a strike, and he was surprised to find himself disappointed rather than relieved.

By midsummer the Amara had rounded into waters further south than Silas had ever imagined existing, and the work had hardened him in ways his mother would not have recognized: his hands calloused past feeling, his skin gone the color of old rope from the sun. A gale in July kept them under close-reefed sails for two days, the whole crew soaked and exhausted and half-convinced the ship would go down, though she rode it out as Thatcher had promised she would. Silas kept a small book in which he wrote, badly, letters to Ruth that he had no way to send until they made a port, describing the flying fish and the strange green fire that sometimes lit the water at night, and asking, on nearly every page, whether she was keeping well and whether she still meant to wait for him.

Their first successful hunt came in September, off a school of sperm whales that Thatcher spotted himself from the masthead, and Silas's boat struck and killed a bull whale after a chase that left every man's arms shaking. It was dangerous work in a way the drills had only half prepared him for; the whale had rolled and nearly staved the boat with a single sweep of its flukes before the harpooner finished it with the lance, and Silas had gone into the water briefly when the boat tipped, hauled back aboard soaked and laughing with the relief particular to men who have just understood how close a thing had been. That night the whole ship worked by torchlight cutting in the carcass, and Silas fell asleep still smelling of oil and blood, feeling, for the first time since New Bedford, entirely like he belonged there.

Two more whales came before winter, and Silas grew steady and useful enough that Thatcher moved him up to bowman in his boat, a mark of trust Silas wrote to Ruth about with more pride than he showed anyone aboard. The work never stopped feeling dangerous, exactly, but it stopped feeling unfamiliar, which men who had done it for years told him was more or less the same thing as safety, though they always said it with a look that suggested they didn't quite believe their own words. He thought often of home during the long stretches between whales, of Ruth's kitchen and his mother's garden, and calculated more than once how many more whales it would take to fill the ship's hold and turn her back toward New Bedford. By his reckoning, if the hunting stayed good, they might see home again within the year.

The whale that found them in February was larger than anything Silas had struck before, an old bull marked with the white scars of past encounters with other boats, which the older hands took as an ill sign rather than simple bad luck for the whale. Thatcher lowered three boats after it in a rising sea, against the mate's quiet advice that the weather looked wrong for it, and Silas's boat took the lead as the whale sounded and came up closer than any of them expected, thrashing in a fury none of the men had seen from a wounded animal before. The harpoon struck true, but the whale did not dive or run as whales usually did; it turned instead, enormous and furious, directly toward the boat, and for a moment every man aboard understood, without needing to say it, that the chase had become something else.

The whale's tail came down across the boat's stern with a sound like a felled tree, splitting the wood and throwing every man into water gone suddenly and violently white with foam and blood. Silas surfaced once, called out, and was pulled under a second time by the boat's own line as it ran out uncontrolled from the tub beneath him, tangling his leg before he could kick free of it. The other boats reached the wreck within minutes and pulled three men from the water alive, but Silas did not come up again, and though they searched the churned sea until the light failed, dragging grapples through the water long after any sensible hope was gone, they found no more of him than his cap, floating upright and strangely undamaged among the wreckage.

The Amara returned to New Bedford eight months later with a full hold and a captain's log that recorded, in Thatcher's cramped hand, the loss of one Silas Coombe, bowman, aged eighteen, lost at sea in the pursuit of a whale off the coast of Patagonia. Ruth Anders was given the news by the ship's agent on the same dock where she had watched Silas sail away, and she kept the small book of unsent letters he had left behind, reading them so many times over the following year that the pages softened like cloth. She never married, though she was asked twice, and she named the modest bakery she eventually opened, twenty years later, simply Coombe's, telling curious customers only that it had been someone's name worth keeping.

Daniel Voss had wanted to be a firefighter since he was nine years old and watched a Chicago engine company pull his neighbor's cat out of a tree, an act of heroism that had nothing to do with fire but had impressed him all the same. Twenty years later, in the autumn of 1985, he was a nine-year veteran of Engine 41 on the city's near west side, thirty-four years old, married to a schoolteacher named Carol, and father to a six-year-old daughter, Beth, who liked to wear his old helmet around the house until it slid down over her eyes. He still felt, most mornings driving to the station, a version of the same excitement he'd felt as a boy, tempered now by a clearer understanding of what the job actually cost, which he tried not to think about too directly on the days Beth hugged him goodbye at the door.

The station ran on routine and bad coffee, and Daniel's closest friend there was Ray Delgado, a broad, cheerful man who had trained him as a rookie and now worked beside him as an equal, a shift in status neither of them had ever bothered to make formal. They spent slow afternoons arguing about baseball and fixing the ancient radio in the common room, and Ray liked to tease Daniel about being the only man on the crew who still wrote thank-you notes to the paramedics after a bad call. Underneath the joking there was a seriousness that surfaced only rarely, usually late at night after a hard fire, when the two of them would sit outside the station in the cold without saying much of anything, letting the adrenaline drain out slowly the way it never quite did in front of the newer guys.

A tenement fire that spring had gone badly wrong when a floor gave way beneath another crew, injuring two men seriously enough that they never returned to active duty, and the department had spent weeks afterward tightening procedures around structural fires in the city's older buildings. Daniel had been on scene that night, had helped carry one of the injured men out himself, and had gone home afterward and sat in Beth's doorway for a long time watching her sleep before Carol found him there and asked, not for the first time, whether he ever thought about a different line of work. He told her, as he always did, that he had thought about it and thought about it and always come back to the same answer, which was that somebody had to do this work and he had decided a long time ago it might as well be him.

Carol Voss taught second grade at a school six blocks from the station and had long ago made peace with the particular anxiety of loving a firefighter, though peace was perhaps too strong a word for the low current of worry that never fully switched off, especially on nights when the wind picked up and made old buildings burn faster and meaner. She kept a small shelf in the kitchen for Daniel's commendations, three of them so far, and joked to her sister that she'd rather have him home and un-decorated, though she never said this to Daniel himself. Beth had started asking, lately, whether her father's job was dangerous, a question Carol answered as honestly as she could manage for a six-year-old, telling her that Daddy and his friends were very well trained and very careful, which was true, and which she hoped would remain enough.

The call came in just after midnight on a Tuesday in November, a four-story apartment building on Ashland Avenue fully involved on the top two floors, with reports of residents still trapped on the third. Engine 41 arrived to find flames already breaking through the roof and a crowd of residents gathered on the sidewalk, several of them shouting that an elderly man in apartment 3C hadn't come down and wasn't answering his door. Daniel and Ray suited up together, as they always did, checking each other's gear with the automatic thoroughness of long habit, and went up the interior stairwell side by side while a second crew worked to knock down the fire from outside. The heat on the third floor was already fierce enough to blister paint on the walls, and visibility had dropped to almost nothing behind a wall of black smoke.

They found the old man in 3C conscious but disoriented, sitting on his bathroom floor where he had gone looking for cooler air, and between them Daniel and Ray got him up and moving toward the stairwell, his weight distributed awkwardly between two men in heavy gear who could barely see past their own hands. The building groaned around them in a way that Daniel, nine years into this work, had learned to take seriously, a sound structural fires made shortly before they made worse sounds. They handed the old man off to a crew coming up to meet them at the second-floor landing, and Ray started down after him immediately, calling back to Daniel that dispatch had just reported a woman in 3D who hadn't been accounted for, and that someone needed to check.

Daniel told Ray to keep going, that he'd check 3D himself and be right behind him, and turned back into the smoke before Ray had finished arguing that they should both go together. He found the door to 3D unlocked and the apartment empty, the woman already accounted for, it turned out, having left an hour earlier to stay with her sister, information the dispatcher had received only moments too late to relay. Daniel radioed that the unit was clear and started back toward the stairwell himself, moving fast now because the heat had climbed sharply in just the few minutes he'd been searching, and the hallway he'd walked through easily before had grown thick and low with smoke that pressed down from a ceiling he could no longer see.

The floor gave way six feet from the stairwell, a section of joists weakened past their limit by heat neither Daniel nor anyone outside could see from below, and he went down with it into the fire on the second floor before the crews working the exterior even registered the sudden collapse in the smoke pattern. Ray was already back inside before anyone told him to be, and it took eleven minutes and two more firefighters to reach the space where Daniel had fallen, eleven minutes that changed nothing about what they found. Daniel Voss was pronounced dead at the scene, the fourteenth line-of-duty death in the department's history that decade, and Engine 41 draped black cloth over its badge for a year, the way custom required, while Ray Delgado carried the old man's rescue and his friend's death as two halves of the same eleven minutes for the rest of his career.

Edmund Calloway rode into the market town of Warkworth in the late summer of 1356 among a column of men bound for the king's muster in France, twenty-six years old and knighted only the previous spring, the ink on his father's approval of the honor barely dry. He had spent the winter training with a sword too heavy for him and a lance he still occasionally dropped, and he carried both now with a confidence that had less to do with skill than with the simple fact that no one had yet told him, in battle, how frightened he was capable of being. His squire, a serious boy named Thomas who had served the Calloway household since childhood, rode a half-length behind him, minding the baggage and the spare horse, and neither of them spoke much of what waited across the sea, preferring instead to argue cheerfully about nothing at all.

That night, camped in a field outside the town with the rest of the muster, Edmund dreamed with a clarity he had never dreamed with before. He stood in a churchyard he did not recognize, gray stone and low mist, and before him was a grave freshly dug, his own name cut into the stone above it in letters too clean for weather to have touched yet. In the dream he understood, without being told, that the ground held him already, that the man walking through the mist and reading his own name was somehow also the man lying beneath it, and the horror of that doubled knowledge woke him gasping before dawn, his blanket soaked through with sweat despite the cold. He lay still for a long while afterward, listening to the ordinary sounds of the camp, and could not shake the certainty that he had been shown something true.

Thomas found him at first light sitting apart from the fire, unusually quiet, and Edmund, after some hesitation, told him about the dream, expecting to be laughed at for a superstitious fool. Thomas did not laugh. He said only that his own grandmother had set great store by such dreams and had always said a man forewarned might yet bend what was coming, though she'd never explained how. Edmund spent the day distracted, checking his gear more carefully than usual, writing a letter to his sister that he sealed and gave to a merchant bound for England before he had fully decided to send it. He told himself, by evening, that a bad dream after too much bad wine meant nothing at all, and that a knight who let visions govern him would never make it through a single campaign, let alone a long one.

The campaign brought Edmund his first real battle within three weeks, a chaotic engagement outside a walled town whose name he would later have trouble remembering clearly, fought in a light rain that turned the field to churned mud within the first hour. He fought well enough, by his own later account and by Thomas's, but a mounted opponent caught him with a glancing blow across the helm that knocked him from his horse and left him briefly unconscious in the mud with men fighting over and around him. He came to with Thomas dragging him bodily toward the rear lines, his ears ringing and one eye swollen shut, convinced for a confused moment, before his senses returned properly, that the dream's grave had finally caught up with him. It had not. He had a concussion, a broken finger, and, as the surgeon told him dryly, considerably more luck than sense.

He spent a week recovering in the baggage train, his head aching and his pride more bruised than his body, turning the dream over and over in his mind now that its threat, for the moment, had passed him by. It occurred to him slowly that the vision had shown him a churchyard he did not recognize, cut with a name he had never actually managed to read clearly no matter how he tried to remember it, and he began to wonder whether he had frightened himself with a nightmare that meant considerably less than it had felt like at three in the morning. Thomas, tending the broken finger with more care than skill, told him plainly that a man could go mad trying to read meaning into every bad dream a campaign produced, and that the sensible thing was to heal, eat something, and get back on his horse.

Edmund returned to fighting within a fortnight, more careful now in ways that had nothing to do with the dream and everything to do with having nearly died from ordinary bad luck rather than any prophecy, which struck him, on reflection, as a more useful lesson than the one he'd originally taken from the nightmare. The campaign ground on through autumn, and he found himself thinking of the churchyard less and less as real memories of real fighting crowded it out, the way a bruise fades and is eventually forgotten by the body even when the mind still remembers being struck. He wrote to his sister again, this time about ordinary things, the weather and the food and a horse he was thinking of buying, and felt, sending it, that he had put something down that he no longer needed to carry.

He came home the following summer with the rest of the muster, sunburned and thinner and carrying a small scar above one eyebrow that would remain the only visible mark the campaign left on him. His sister had arranged, in his absence, an introduction to a merchant's daughter named Alys, whom Edmund found he liked considerably more than he had expected to like anyone his sister arranged for him, and they were married within the year in the same parish church Edmund had been christened in. He told Alys about the dream once, early in their marriage, half expecting her to think less of him for having been so shaken by it, but she only asked whether he still believed it meant anything, and he found, answering her, that he could honestly say he did not.

Edmund Calloway lived to be an old man by the standards of his century, sixty-one years old when he finally died in his own bed in the house he had built for Alys, surrounded by three grown children and a scattering of grandchildren who had heard the story of the churchyard dream so many times it had become a kind of family joke, one Edmund himself told with relish at every retelling. He was buried, in the end, not in the gray churchyard of his nightmare but in the sunlit one beside his own parish, under a stone that named him plainly and correctly, and Thomas, who outlived him by only two years and had never stopped believing the dream had meant something, stood at the graveside remembering the frightened young knight who had once woken him before dawn, certain the ground already held him.

Clara Whitfield had been a nurse at St. Bartholomew's for six years by the autumn of 1940, and nothing in that training had quite prepared her for London under nightly bombardment, though she supposed nothing could have. She was twenty-nine, unmarried, having postponed more than one engagement for the sake of her work, and she had grown used to sleeping in short, interrupted stretches in a basement ward converted for the purpose, waking at the sound of the siren before she was even fully aware she'd heard it. Her patients came in a steady, terrible variety, burns and crush injuries and the shock that sometimes killed people who had no visible wound at all, and Clara moved among them with a calm she had built deliberately, piece by piece, because she had noticed early on that patients healed better around nurses who did not appear frightened.

The raids fell into a grim rhythm that autumn, and Clara's own rhythm bent itself around theirs: sleep when the sirens allowed it, eat when there was time, and work through nights that stretched past any reasonable measure of a shift. She had a close friend among the other nurses, a sharp-tongued young woman named Peggy Marsh, and the two of them had developed a habit of sharing a cigarette on the hospital steps in the gray hour after a raid ended, saying very little, simply glad to be standing upright in air that didn't smell of dust and cordite for a few minutes. Clara had lost patients before that autumn, more than she let herself count too carefully, but she had not yet lost anyone she loved, and some small, unexamined part of her still believed, the way the young often do, that this arrangement might continue.

She fell ill herself in November, a fever that came on fast after two days of unbroken work following a particularly bad raid near the docks, and Peggy, alarmed at how quickly Clara's condition worsened, insisted on putting her to bed in the nurses' quarters rather than letting her sleep it off in a chair as Clara wanted to. The fever climbed through the night despite everything the on-duty doctor tried, and by the following evening Clara was delirious enough that she no longer recognized Peggy's voice reliably, drifting between a version of the ward that was real and one that had begun, disturbingly, to bend and repeat itself in ways that made no sense. The doctor used the word dangerous within Peggy's hearing, quietly, the way doctors did when they didn't want a patient's friends to fully understand how dangerous.

In the deepest part of the fever, Clara dreamed she was standing at her own funeral, watching from just outside the small gathering as Peggy read something from a folded piece of paper in a voice gone flat with grief, and her mother, whom Clara had not seen in eight months, stood at the graveside in a coat too thin for the weather. She could see her own name on the temporary marker, spelled correctly, which seemed in the dream like a small, absurd mercy, and she felt, watching the scene, not fear exactly but a strange, heavy sorrow at how ordinary it all looked, how easily the world seemed to be managing without her. She tried to call out to Peggy, to say that she was still there, still watching, and could not make her voice work in the dream any better than she could make it work through the fever itself.

The fever broke on the third night, suddenly, the way bad fevers sometimes do, and Clara woke to find Peggy asleep in the chair beside her bed, still in her uniform, having refused for two days to go off duty for more than an hour at a time. Clara's throat was too raw to speak properly, but she managed to say Peggy's name, and Peggy woke with a start and then, seeing Clara's eyes clear and focused for the first time in days, began to cry in a way she would later deny entirely. Clara spent the next week recovering slowly, weaker than she had ever felt in her adult life, and told Peggy, once she had the strength for a full sentence, about the dream of the funeral, expecting to be told it meant nothing, which Peggy told her immediately and firmly, adding that she'd had quite enough of funerals lately without imagining new ones.

She was back on the ward within three weeks, thinner and more easily tired than before but otherwise recovered, and she found the dream stayed with her afterward in a way that surprised her, not as a fear exactly but as a kind of measuring stick. She noticed she had stopped taking the ordinary continuation of her own life for granted in quite the automatic way she once had, and she began, in small ways, doing things she had been postponing: writing properly to her mother instead of brief notes, telling Peggy outright how much her two nights in that chair had meant. The war went on being the war regardless of what Clara had or had not learned from a fever dream, and she returned to the work of it with the same careful calm as before, if perhaps a little more grateful for each ordinary morning that arrived.

A raid in the spring brought the hospital itself under threat for the first time, an incendiary landing on the roof two floors above the ward where Clara was working, and for a chaotic quarter of an hour the possibility of the funeral dream felt uncomfortably close as smoke began filling the stairwell and patients had to be moved by hand to the far wing. Clara worked through it without letting herself think about the dream at all, focused entirely on the next patient and the next, and the fire brigade had the blaze out before it reached beyond the roof space, leaving the ward smoke-stained but intact. Afterward, sitting on the steps with Peggy in the gray hour that had become their habit, Clara said only that she was getting rather tired of buildings trying to fall on her, and Peggy said she'd noticed the same thing about the whole war.

Clara Whitfield stayed at St. Bartholomew's through the rest of the war and for another twenty years after it, eventually training three generations of nurses in the same wards where she had once nursed the Blitz's wounded, and she told the story of the fever dream only rarely, usually to junior nurses who seemed to need reminding that surviving something frightening was not the same as being broken by it. Peggy remained her closest friend for the whole of both their long lives, and at Clara's actual funeral, decades later, at the genuine age of eighty-four, it was Peggy's daughter who read the eulogy, since Peggy herself had died two years before, and who mentioned, because Clara had asked her to include it, a dream her mother's oldest friend had once survived by simply waking up and going back to work.

Magnus Halvorsen joined the Norwegian expedition bound for the interior of Svalbard in the spring of 1911, one of six men tasked with mapping a stretch of glacier that no expedition had yet crossed on foot. He was thirty-two, a former merchant sailor who had switched to polar work after deciding the sea held no more surprises for him, a decision his wife back in Tromso still teased him about in her letters, since the ice, she pointed out, seemed to hold rather more danger than the sea ever had. The expedition leader, a stern but fair man named Erik Solberg, had chosen Magnus specifically for his steadiness under pressure, a reputation earned on an earlier voyage when a fire below deck had been contained largely because Magnus refused to panic while everyone around him did. They set out from the coastal station with dog sledges and six months of careful planning behind them.

Three weeks into the crossing, with the party camped at the base of a long ridge they intended to survey the following morning, Magnus volunteered to scout ahead alone while there was still light, a routine enough task that no one thought twice about it. A storm that the expedition's instruments had given no serious warning of rolled in from the northwest within the hour, dropping visibility to almost nothing and turning the flat, featureless ice into a white blur in every direction. Solberg fired signal flares at intervals through the worst of it, a standard procedure for exactly this situation, but the wind swallowed the light almost as fast as it appeared, and by the time the storm finally broke, twelve hours later, Magnus had not returned to camp, and his tracks, when the men searched for them, ended abruptly at a ridge where the wind had scoured the snow clean.

The search that followed was as thorough as six exhausted men and a limited store of daylight could make it, spreading out in careful lines across a landscape that offered almost nothing to distinguish one stretch of ice from another. They found no sign of him on the first day, none on the second, and by the third, Solberg was forced to weigh the search against the party's dwindling supplies and the real danger of losing more men to the same storm that had likely taken Magnus. He extended the search twice past what the expedition's own protocols recommended, unwilling to be the one who gave the order to stop, and it was only when a second smaller storm began building on the horizon that he finally called the men back toward the main camp, radioing the coastal station with a report that used the word missing rather than the word he privately feared was more accurate.

Word reached Tromso by wireless relay ten days later, garbled and delayed enough in transmission that Magnus's wife, Ingrid, first understood only that her husband was missing and presumed lost in a storm, with no further detail offered because none, at that point, existed to offer. She kept the letters he had sent over the winter in a drawer by the bed and read them again that week more than she had read them when they first arrived, looking, she admitted to her sister, for anything in his ordinary complaints about cold rations that might now read as some kind of goodbye. The expedition's sponsors in Oslo began drafting a notice for the newspapers that referred to Magnus in the past tense, a formality Solberg fought against by wireless for as long as he reasonably could, insisting there was still no confirmed body and therefore, in his own stubborn accounting, still no confirmed death.

Back at the ice, the second storm delayed any further search for four more days, and when it finally cleared, Solberg led a smaller party back out toward the ridge more out of a sense of obligation to Ingrid than any real hope, telling the others privately that they were now searching for a body to bring home rather than a man to rescue. They found the ridge exactly as bleak and empty as before, and Solberg stood at the spot where Magnus's tracks had vanished for a long time, turning over in his mind how he would write to a wife he had never met about a man he had personally recruited into this. It was one of the younger men, scanning the terrain out of simple restlessness rather than any particular instinct, who noticed a dark irregularity half a mile off that did not match the pattern of any rock formation on their maps.

The irregularity turned out to be a low ridge of pressure ice that had folded over itself during the original storm, creating a narrow, wind-sheltered pocket beneath an overhang, and inside it, when the search party finally reached it, they found Magnus alive, badly frostbitten and weak from ten days on almost no food, but alive and, astonishingly, still able to speak when they reached him. He had followed his own training when the storm hit, digging into the first shelter he could find rather than trying to walk blind through it, and had rationed the small emergency store every sledge carried into portions that had kept him breathing but had left almost nothing to spare by the time they found him. He asked, before he asked anything else, whether Solberg had sent word to Ingrid yet that he was missing, and seemed more distressed by the thought of her worrying than by his own ten days in the ice.

They carried him back to the main camp on an improvised sledge, and the expedition's doctor, examining him by lamplight that first night, gave a guarded assessment that he would likely keep all his fingers and most of his toes, though it would be a slow recovery, and that the greater danger now was simply the exhaustion and cold his body had absorbed over ten days rather than any single injury. Solberg wired the coastal station immediately with a correction to his earlier report, using, this time, the word alive with a bluntness that the station operator later said had made him laugh out loud with relief in an otherwise empty radio room. The message took another ten days to reach Tromso through the same relay chain that had delivered the bad news, and Ingrid, reading it, sat down on the kitchen floor because her legs would no longer hold her upright.

Magnus returned to Tromso six weeks later, walking with a cane and missing the smallest toe on his left foot, to a homecoming considerably larger than the quiet arrival he had originally planned for after a routine mapping expedition. Ingrid met him at the dock and did not let go of his arm for the better part of an hour, and Solberg, who had come south with him, stood back and let the reunion happen without him, satisfied simply to have been wrong about what he'd expected to be delivering. Magnus never went back to that particular stretch of glacier, though he returned to Arctic work twice more in later years, and he kept, for the rest of his life, a small piece of the pressure ice's shelter wall sketched from memory in his expedition journal, a reminder, he told his children, of exactly how much ten days of careful rationing could be worth.

Grace Okafor was thirty-one and two years into running her own small architecture practice in Lagos when a client meeting on the mainland ran late enough that she left the office well after dark, tired in the specific way that came from arguing for an hour about a roofline nobody else seemed to think mattered as much as she did. She had grown up in Surulere and moved back there after university abroad, partly out of homesickness and partly out of a conviction, which she defended cheerfully at every family gathering, that Lagos needed architects who actually understood how the city worked rather than importing ideas that assumed different weather and different money. Her mother called while she was still at the office, as she did most evenings, to remind her that dinner was getting cold and that no roofline was worth skipping a meal for, and Grace promised, laughing, that she was leaving that very minute.

She was two kilometers from home, waiting at a junction she had crossed a thousand times before, when a bus running the wrong side of a poorly lit roundabout struck the side of her car with enough force to spin it into the median barrier. Grace did not lose consciousness immediately; she remembered, in the fragmented way accident survivors often do, the sound of the impact and then a strange, muffled quiet, and being aware that something was very wrong with her own breathing before the awareness itself dissolved into nothing. A motorcycle rider who had witnessed the crash called for help and stayed with the car until an ambulance arrived, information Grace would only learn much later, secondhand, from a hospital report that described her condition on arrival as critical, with significant internal injuries and a head trauma severe enough that the emergency team moved her directly into surgery without waiting for her family to arrive.

Grace's mother reached the hospital before her father did, having been called by a nurse using a number found on Grace's phone, and spent the first three hours in a corridor with no information beyond the fact that her daughter was in surgery and that the surgery was serious. When the surgeon finally came out, he used careful, measured language about the next forty-eight hours being critical, about swelling in the brain that they were monitoring closely, about the very real possibility that Grace might not wake up even if the surgery itself had gone as well as it could. Grace's father arrived to find his wife sitting perfectly still in a plastic chair, and when he asked what the doctor had said, she could only repeat the phrase critical condition several times before she was able to add anything further, as though the words themselves had used up everything she had left.

Grace remained unconscious for six days in the intensive care unit, her condition described each morning to her waiting family in terms that shifted only slightly from one day to the next, stable but critical, then critical but stable, distinctions that felt meaningless to people who simply wanted to know whether she would live. Her mother did not leave the hospital for more than an hour at a stretch during that week, sleeping when she slept in the same plastic chair, and Grace's younger brother flew back from a job in Abuja to sit with the family in shifts that none of them coordinated formally but that somehow ensured someone was always in the corridor. A pastor from the family's church came twice to pray over Grace's unconscious body, and on the fourth day, when a monitor alarm sounded briefly during a routine check, the entire family stood outside the ICU doors in a silence none of them later found words to describe.

On the sixth day, a doctor came out with a different tone than the family had grown used to, careful still but noticeably less guarded, explaining that the swelling had begun to reduce and that Grace's responses to basic stimuli, checked regularly through the worst of it, had started showing small but real improvement overnight. Grace's mother asked, three separate times in three slightly different ways, whether this meant her daughter would wake up, and the doctor, more honestly than doctors always allowed themselves to be, said that it meant the odds had shifted meaningfully in that direction, though nothing was certain until it happened. The family allowed themselves, for the first time in a week, to speak to each other in something other than the flattened, careful tone they had all adopted, and Grace's brother went out to the hospital canteen and bought food for everyone, an ordinary act that felt, that day, like an enormous one.

Grace opened her eyes on the seventh day, briefly and without full clarity at first, aware mainly of brightness and of a hand holding hers that turned out to be her mother's, and it took another two days of intermittent, confused waking before she could hold a conversation longer than a few words. She remembered nothing of the crash itself and very little of the days immediately before it, a gap her doctors told her was common and would likely never fully fill in, but she recognized her family without hesitation, which the medical team treated as the most encouraging sign yet. Her mother cried harder seeing Grace fully awake and asking, in a raspy but recognizably impatient voice, why everyone was staring at her like that, than she had cried at any point during the six days of not knowing, relief arriving, it turned out, with its own particular force.

Recovery took months rather than days, physical therapy for a leg that had been badly broken and speech therapy for a brief period when Grace's words came out scrambled in ways that frightened her more than anything the accident itself had done. She moved back in with her parents for the duration of it, something she had not done since university, and found there was a strange comfort in being fussed over by her mother in the same house she'd grown up in, even as she chafed, increasingly as she improved, against being treated like someone fragile. Her business partner kept the practice running in her absence and brought her small design problems to solve from her parents' dining table as she got stronger, a gesture Grace understood, gratefully, as her partner's way of reminding her who she still was underneath the injuries, a reminder she needed more than she admitted to anyone.

A year after the accident, Grace walked with only a barely noticeable limp that mostly showed up when she was tired, and she had gone back to running her practice full time, including a small addition to the design of a community center that she insisted on including specifically because of a junction visibility issue she now understood in a way she never had before the crash. She still called her mother every evening on her way home, a habit that had started as her mother's anxious requirement and had become, over the year, something Grace found she wanted just as much. On the anniversary of the crash, quietly and without telling her family, she visited the roundabout where it had happened, stood there for a few minutes in the ordinary evening traffic, and then drove the rest of the way home exactly as she always had.
